issues.legal_issue: A hereditary trustee’s bare right to manage and administer an institution’s secular estate, without a beneficial or proprietary interest in the estate, is not property protected by the constitutional right to hold property.
material_facts: The hereditary trustees claimed only the right to manage and administer the secular estate of the institutions and endowments.
They did not claim a proprietary or beneficial interest in the property or its income.
The trustees succeeded to their offices by hereditary succession, but their duties and obligations otherwise resembled those of a manager or custodian.
issues.conclusion: The office of hereditary trustee, in these circumstances, is not property within the meaning of Article 19(1)(f) or any other constitutional provision.
issues.legal_principle: A bare right to manage an institution or endowment, without a beneficial interest in its property, is not property for constitutional protection. The Court followed Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan and Raja Birakishore v. State of Orissa, and distinguished the broader rights of a shebait, mahant or mathadhipati. It treated the statement in Sambudamurthi Mudaliar v. State of Madras that hereditary trusteeship is in the nature of property as obiter, and considered the Privy Council decisions applying the Tagore rule to succession to hereditary offices unhelpful to the constitutional question.

predicates.constitutional_appeal_challenging_truste: An appeal challenging statutory controls over the management of an institution or endowment as unconstitutional is before the court.
predicates.bare_management_right: The office-holder claims only a right to manage and administer the institution’s or endowment’s estate.
predicates.no_beneficial_or_proprietary_interest: The office-holder claims no beneficial or proprietary interest in the estate or its income.
predicates.hereditary_trustee_office_is_not_constit: The hereditary office-holder’s bare management right is not property protected by the constitutional right to hold property.

issues.definition: When a constitutional appeal concerns an office-holder who claims only management authority and no beneficial or proprietary interest, the office is not treated as constitutionally protected property.

issues.legal_issue: Statutory controls requiring hereditary trustees to share secular administration with other trustees and executive officers are reasonable and in the public interest when they preserve the hereditary trustee’s office and do not interfere with religious functions.
material_facts: The challenged provisions permitted the appointment of non-hereditary trustees and executive officers even where hereditary trustees were in office and no mismanagement had been found.
A hereditary trustee was not removed from office and was to chair the board, alone or by rotation where there was more than one hereditary trustee.
The controls required administration in collaboration with other trustees and placed aspects of management with an executive officer.
The challenged controls concerned secular administration; religious practices and functions were to continue according to the applicable religious rules, usage or custom.
A commission had reported widespread mismanagement of endowment property and misuse of endowment funds.
issues.conclusion: Even if the hereditary trustees’ rights constituted property, the restrictions imposed by the Act were reasonable and in the interest of the general public.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(5) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The Court held that associating non-hereditary trustees and executive officers with management served the purpose of better and more efficient administration; hereditary trustees retained their office and a chairmanship role, and religious matters were not interfered with. Sections 15, 17, 27, 36 and 97 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, were among the challenged provisions. The Court relied on the reported need to address mismanagement and misuse of endowment property.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns statutory management controls that improve public administration, preserve the hereditary trustee’s office and chair role, and leave religious functions untouched, the controls are reasonable and in the public interest.
